content.title: About
content.content: Black beans (Phaseolus vulgaris) are dried seeds of the common bean, widely used in Latin American, Caribbean, and US cuisines. They have a dense, meaty texture, a mildly nutty flavor, and turn a deep black color when cooked.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Black beans are sometimes called “black soybeans,” although they are not related to soy.
In the United States they are a staple of Southern dishes such as “beans and rice.”
They are rich in anthocyanins, the pigments that give them their dark color and antioxidant properties.
Traditional dishes include arroz con frijoles negros, salads, and vegetarian patties.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: One cup of cooked black beans provides about 15 g of protein, making them an excellent protein source for vegetarians.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains iron and folate
items.content: These nutrients are essential for blood formation and preventing anemia, especially in women of childbearing age.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Black beans raise blood glucose slowly, which is beneficial for diabetes management and weight control.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Anthocyanins and other polyphenols protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Present in beans and can reduce mineral absorption; soaking and thorough cooking mitigate this.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Beans may cause gastrointestinal discomfort in sensitive individuals; gradual introduction helps.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to beans.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Black beans can be boiled, stewed, added to soups, salads, chili, burritos, or blended into spreads. Soak the dry beans for at least 6 hours, then simmer 45–60 minutes until tender.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry beans in an airtight container in a cool, dry place for up to 1 year. Cooked beans keep 3–5 days in the refrigerator and up to 3 months in the freezer.
